analysis.one_liner: Automatically enrolls every child born after 2002 in a new Medicare-style health plan through age 23.
analysis.headline: A bill to guarantee government health coverage for every child born after 2002, with 66 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote and expired when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: MediKids would have created a public health insurance program, run like Medicare, that every child born after December 31, 2002 is enrolled in at birth and keeps until age 23. Benefits would include everything Medicaid requires for children plus prescription drugs, with no cost-sharing for the poorest families. Families would pay a monthly premium through their tax return, exempt or reduced for low incomes and capped at 5 percent of income, with future progressive tax changes to cover the cost as enrollment grew. The bill never left House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Children born after 2002, who would carry guaranteed coverage from birth through age 23 regardless of their parents' job changes, income swings, or moves between states. The bill's own findings cite more than 11 million uninsured children. Low-income families benefit most: no cost-sharing below 150 percent of the poverty line, premium exemptions for very low incomes, and a refundable credit covering half of cost-sharing for other low-income families. Families with children in Medicaid or SCHIP keep those programs, with MediKids as a backstop whenever other coverage lapses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, especially uninsured and low-income kids

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after 2002 would be deemed enrolled at birth and entitled to comprehensive coverage until age 23, with the eligible age range phasing in over five years until it reaches everyone under 23.

Benefits would include all services Medicaid requires for children, including early and periodic screening, diagnosis, and treatment, plus prescription drugs and biologicals, and at least the core Medicare benefits.

Children in families below 150 percent of the poverty line would pay no cost-sharing, taxpayers with very low incomes would be exempt from premiums, and families would get a refundable credit for half of cost-sharing expenses.

The bill's findings state that more than 11 million American children are uninsured, and that uninsured children receive less preventive care and have poorer health, imposing lifetime costs on themselves and the economy.
Families could keep private coverage, Medicaid, or SCHIP with zero MediKids premium for any month they demonstrate equivalent coverage, so MediKids acts as a default safety net rather than a mandate.

analysis.who_pays: Families with enrolled children pay a monthly premium collected through their tax return, capped at 5 percent of adjusted gross income and phased out for very low incomes. The program would be funded from those premiums plus appropriations into a new MediKids Trust Fund, and the Treasury Secretary would be required to propose a schedule of progressive tax changes as enrollment grows. Providers would be paid on Medicare-like schedules, which generally pay less than private insurance rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new premium tax on families with enrolled children, collected through tax filing, that in no case exceeds 5 percent of adjusted gross income, with exemptions only for the lowest incomes.

Coverage phases in only for children born after December 31, 2002, expanding by age brackets over five years, so it would take more than two decades before the whole under-23 population is covered, leaving today's uninsured children out.

The HHS Secretary would specify the benefit package and payment schedule with wide discretion, and benefits could be delivered through private Medicare+Choice-style plans whose rates would be adjusted by the Secretary, adding administrative complexity and private-plan involvement to a new entitlement.

States would be barred from rolling back Medicaid and SCHIP eligibility or benefits for anyone under 23, and would have to spend any savings from children shifting to MediKids on improving Medicaid services, a condition some states could find restrictive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The guarantee is broad and the cost-sharing protections for poor families are strong, but the design asks every family with a covered child to pay a new premium even at middle incomes, and the birth-year phase-in means the sickest uninsured children of 2001 would get nothing. The benefit package rests heavily on discretionary HHS rulemaking rather than statutory detail, which makes the promise dependent on future administrations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, handed down to their health subcommittees within two weeks, and never reported out, so it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the MediKids Health Insurance Act on May 3, 2001, joined by 11 original cosponsors including Reps. Rangel, George Miller, McDermott, and Conyers.
The bill drew 66 cosponsors: 64 of 208 House Democrats, the chamber's sole Independent, and 1 of 223 House Republicans.
It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on May 3, 2001; on May 10 it went to the Trade Subcommittee and on May 15 to the Health Subcommittee of Ways and Means.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo was preserved: children who were uninsured in 2001 remained without a guaranteed safety net, and no committee or member ever had to cast a recorded vote on creating the program or on the taxes and premiums that would fund it. Insurers and employers kept covering children on market terms rather than facing a public default plan competing with them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The coverage status quo and its insurers

sides.party_line_note: No one ever voted on the bill, so there is no opposition record; the 66 cosponsors were almost entirely Democrats (64 of 208, plus the chamber's one Independent and just 1 of 223 Republicans), suggesting a heavily partisan support base without a corresponding on-the-record opposition.

industries.note: A public MediKids default plan would displace private coverage for children whenever families chose or fell into it, cutting private premium revenue, but the bill also allows benefits to be delivered through private Medicare+Choice-style plans paid capitation rates set by the Secretary. Insurers would lose market share to a public program while gaining a possible new publicly funded customer channel.

Eleven million uninsured children becoming enrolled patients means fewer unpaid emergency-room cases and more paid visits, though Medicare-style payment schedules would generally pay providers less than private rates.
The benefit package must include prescription drugs and biologicals for all enrolled children, creating a large new pool of covered pediatric drug purchases paid through the trust fund.
